newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela abandons search for quake survivors.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela abandons search for quake survivors.

text.p: Abandoning the hunt for survivors, rescue teams in eastern Venezuela on Saturday concentrated on retrieving the victims of a powerful quake that killed at least 72, many of them children crushed at their school desks.
Three days after the quake struck, the rigid corpse of a 27-year-old-woman, seven months pregnant, was pulled from the ruins of what was once a 6-storey building.
The discovery brought the number killed in Wednesday's tremor to 72, Civil Defence officials said. The toll was expected to rise as more bodies were uncovered, they said.

"We're not looking for survivors any more, just corpses," said fireman Jose Munoz as he watched colleagues with bulldozers and jack hammers dig through the mound of concrete and girders that was once an office building in the Sucre state capital Cumana, 255 miles (410 km) east of Caracas.
Despite intense efforts -- including pumping oxygen into the building to keep survivors alive -- rescuers have not pulled anybody out alive since Thursday morning.
Nearly 500 people were injured and more than 700 homes flattened in the quake which measured 6.9 on the Richter scale, state Governor Ramon Martinez said.

The pregnant body of Rosa Mercedes Bermudez was found pinned under a beam in the fourth floor office where she had worked as a secretary. Bermudez was the 24th person known to have died in the building.
Another nine bodies are thought to be trapped in the bowels of the wreckage, including 5-year-old twins and their 16-year-old baby-sitter.

Worst-hit by the quake -- Venezuela's deadliest for three decades -- was the small agricultural town Cariaco, 40 miles (64 km) east of Cumana, where a high school and nursery school fell on pupils and teachers.
Many of the pupils were taking end-of-term exams when the roof caved in. Friday would have been the first day of their summer break.

A bulldozer cleared away the school's ruins Saturday. At least 42 bodies were recovered from among the fallen masonry and scattered exercise books. Two-year-old infants and an 81-year-old man were among the dead.
Hours after the quake rescuers found two girls, still alive, huddled under the lifeless body of 39-year-old teacher Madeleine de Sanchez, locals said.
Cariaco, a tiny town of 13,000, bore the brunt of the quake, which devastated three quarters of its mud-walled, straw-roofed homes which crumpled the instant the tremor hit.

Residents spent Friday night sleeping in makeshift tents and under plastic sheets in the narrow streets. Aid in the form of mattresses, food and drinking water began to arrive late on Friday but the town still remained without power and running water.
The tiny hospital was evacuated on Thursday due to fears it too might collapse.
The government approved an initial budget of $15 million to repair damage from the quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967 when 300 people died.
